lifeboat_capacity.name: Davit Capacity Settled

description.text: Twenty boats: seats for barely half of those who will sail.
A boat on every davit: seats for everyone aboard.

description: In the drawing office at Harland & Wolff, the question of how many lifeboats Titanic will carry is settled for the last time.

description.text: Her Welin davits were designed to handle as many as 64 boats, but the Board of Trade requires only 16 for any ship over 10,000 tons.
Uncluttered promenade decks win the argument over boats that the rules do not require.

roster_reshuffle.name: Roster Reshuffle

description.text: Wilde takes over as chief officer and Blair leaves the ship.
The officers sail as first appointed, and Blair stays aboard.
No one thinks to ask Blair for his keys.
Before he goes ashore, Blair is reminded to hand over the crow’s nest key.
The locker key stays ashore with Blair.
The locker key is aboard when she sails.

description: Days before sailing, White Star reshuffles Titanic’s senior officers, bringing Henry Wilde across from the Olympic as chief officer.

description.text: Second Officer David Blair is bumped from the voyage entirely. He goes ashore with the key to the crow’s nest locker still in his pocket.
The binoculars in that locker are meant for the lookouts.

titanic_departs.name: Boarding & Departure
description: Passengers and crew board at Southampton, and at noon Titanic slips her moorings for Cherbourg, Queenstown and New York.

description.text: As she passes, her wash snaps the mooring lines of the SS New York, which swings to within a few feet of Titanic’s stern.
She will carry more than 2,200 people, and lifeboat seats for barely half of them.
She will carry more than 2,200 people, and a lifeboat seat for every one of them.

ice_warnings.name: Ice Warnings Received

description.text: Most warnings are logged and pinned up; few reach the bridge in time to be useful.
This time the warning is carried to the officer of the watch.

description: Throughout the day the Marconi “radio” operators receive ice warnings from ships ahead.

description.text: Caronia, Baltic, Amerika and Californian all report ice across the ship’s track. Not every message is taken to the bridge.
At 21:40 the Mesaba reports heavy pack ice and great numbers of large icebergs directly in Titanic’s path.

purser_spare.name: The Purser’s Spare

description.text: The spare glasses stay in the drawer.
The spare glasses are found and sent up to the crow’s nest.

description: In the purser’s office the evening passes with the ordinary business of a liner: valuables lodged, cabins changed, telegrams paid for.

description.text: The lookouts have asked for binoculars and been told there are none to be had.
A pair of glasses, left behind by a departing officer, sits unclaimed in a drawer of the office.

wireless_priority.name: Marconi Traffic Backlog

description.text: The traffic runs late, and the Californian’s operator goes to bed before Titanic calls for help.
The backlog is clear early, and the Californian’s operator is still listening when the call goes out.

description: Having lost hours to a fault in the set, Jack Phillips and Harold Bride are far behind on passengers’ private telegrams.

description.text: Within range of the station at Cape Race at last, Phillips works through the backlog at full speed.
Near 23:00 the Californian breaks in to say she is stopped in ice. Phillips cuts her off: “Shut up, shut up, I am busy; I am working Cape Race.”
Soon after, the Californian’s only wireless operator switches off his set and turns in for the night.

missing_binoculars.name: Missing Binoculars

description.text: No key has been left in the nest.
A key to the locker is waiting in the nest when the watch begins.
The locker stays shut.
The locker has been picked open.
The lookouts search the dark with their naked eyes.
The lookouts have binoculars.

description: Through the late watches, the lookouts in the crow’s nest search a moonless, flat-calm sea.

description.text: The glasses meant for them are in a locker in the nest itself, and the key left the ship at Southampton.
With no swell breaking at its base, an iceberg on such a night shows almost nothing until it is close.

engine_order.name: Full Astern

description.text: Her engines go astern, and she answers the helm sluggishly.
Her engines keep driving ahead, and she answers the helm hard.

description: Far below the waterline, the engineers keep Titanic steaming at close to 22 knots through the dark.

description.text: At 23:40 the telegraph rings down to stop, then full astern.
With the engines reversing, the centre turbine stops, and the rudder loses the wash of the screw just ahead of it.

lookout_sights_berg.name: Berg Sighted

description.text: The berg is seen far too late to avoid.
The berg is seen early, with time for the bridge to act.

description: Lookout Frederick Fleet sees a dark mass dead ahead, strikes the bell three times and telephones the bridge: “Iceberg right ahead.”

description.text: First Officer William Murdoch orders her hard a-starboard. The berg is barely a quarter of a mile away.
The berg is seen miles off, and the bridge has minutes, not seconds, to steer clear.
She clears the berg without a mark on her.
The iceberg tears open her starboard bow.
At 23:40 Titanic’s starboard bow scrapes along the iceberg. The contact lasts only seconds.
At 23:40 Titanic swings clear of the iceberg and steams on through the ice field.
The ice opens her first five watertight compartments to the sea. She can float with no more than four flooded.
Thomas Andrews, her designer, inspects the damage and gives her an hour, perhaps an hour and a half.

californian_nearby.name: The Californian Stands By

description.text: Her operator is asleep, and the rockets go unexplained.
Her operator hears the distress call, and she raises steam for the rescue.

description: Stopped for the night at the edge of the ice field, the Leyland liner Californian lies close enough for her officers to see a ship’s lights to the south.

description.text: Her officers of the watch see white rockets burst above the stranger and report them below. No one wakes the wireless operator.
By the time she learns the truth the next morning, the Carpathia has already picked up the survivors.
Almost everyone aboard survives the night.
More than 1,500 lives are lost.
At 02:20 Titanic’s stern rises, hangs, and slides beneath the surface. More than 1,500 people are left in water below freezing.
Titanic founders at 02:20, but she goes down with a seat in a boat for everyone and the Californian standing by.
At 02:20 the boat deck is quiet: a late promenade on a cold, clear night aboard a ship bound for New York.
Twenty boats leave the ship, many of them half full. The Carpathia, racing from 58 miles away, will not arrive until after 04:00.
In a single night, the lifeboat rules for every ship at sea are shown to be written for a world that no longer exists.
